title: Best Affirmation Apps for Shame and Guilt in 2026
description: The best affirmation apps for shame and guilt in 2026, compared by whether their sentences separate an act you regret from a verdict on the whole self, whether you can write a believable line yourself, whether they reach you in the replay minute before the third apology or the disappearance, and what they cost over a year — with the shame–guilt distinction and compassion research stated plainly.
markdown:
By Anicca · November 2026

"Best affirmation app" is the wrong question when what you actually have is not a shortage of positivity but a verdict that will not stop replaying. You said the wrong thing in the meeting — or you did not say it wrong, you cannot even tell any more — and three days later the moment is still running, except now it is no longer about the sentence. It is about you. Not "that came out badly" but "I am the kind of person who ruins rooms". Not "I forgot, and that had a cost" but "I am careless, I am selfish, I am bad". You apologise a second and third time, long after the other person has moved on, not because the apology is owed but because the feeling needs somewhere to go. Or you go the other way: you avoid the person, the inbox, the place, because being seen feels like the punishment itself. That slide — from an act you regret to a self you condemn — is what changes what an app has to do, and it rules out most of what affirmation apps sell. A person in shame does not need a larger claim about the self — "I am a wonderful person", "I accept myself completely" — because the self is exactly what is on trial, and a grand acquittal from an app carries no evidence, so the mind cross-examines it and returns a harsher verdict. What can help, modestly and honestly, is narrower: words that separate the act from the person — "that sentence landed badly, and I can repair that sentence", "a bad hour is evidence about an hour" — written at a size you can actually believe, in a tone of warmth rather than triumph, arriving in the minute the replay starts, from an app that never converts a hiding week into a broken streak. The apps below are therefore not ranked by who praises you most. They are ranked by what still helps, honestly, when one moment has been read as a verdict on the whole person and your hands are already moving toward the third apology — or toward disappearing. This comparison follows the same form as our roundups of the best affirmation apps for anxiety, for sleep and racing thoughts at night, for self-esteem and low self-worth, for stress and overwhelm, for overthinking and rumination, for imposter syndrome and the fraud feeling at work, for perfectionism and the flawless-or-failure loop, for social anxiety and the replay after conversations, for burnout and exhaustion that rest does not fix, for a breakup and the urge to check their profile, for grief after the death of someone you love, for depression and persistently low mood, for people-pleasing and the fear of disapproval, for health anxiety and the search-check-reassure loop, for loneliness and the quiet room at night, and for OCD and intrusive thoughts, re-aimed at shame and guilt and the replay that turns an act into a verdict.

*Disclosure: Anicca, the app listed sixth here, is made by the team behind this site. It is not ranked first. No app paid to be here. Prices and ratings are from the US App Store listings when we checked on November 20, 2026; check the store page for your country. Two boundaries before the list itself. First: shame and guilt are emotions, not diagnoses, and feeling them — even strongly, even often — is not an illness and does not make you a bad person; guilt about a specific act, in proportion, is one of the ways people stay kind, as the research section below sets out. Second: no app on this page is a treatment for anything, including our own app. Where shame arrives fused with depression, trauma, an eating disorder, or thoughts of harming yourself, that is a reason to talk to a clinician or, in a crisis, your local emergency number or crisis line now — in the US, call or text 988; in Japan, call 110 or 119 in an emergency. What follows is a comparison of self-help tools for the replay minute, written for people who are also, where they need it, getting real help.*

## How we judged these, for shame and guilt specifically

1. **Can you write a sentence that separates the act from the self?** This is the first filter, and most affirmation content fails it. The distinction the research starts from, set out by Lewis and developed empirically by Tangney and colleagues, is that guilt evaluates a behaviour — "I did a bad thing" — while shame evaluates the whole self — "I am bad" (Tangney, Stuewig & Mashek, 2007). The two feel similar and they push opposite ways: guilt, kept about an act, tends toward apology, repair and changed behaviour; shame tends toward hiding, shrinking and disappearing. Read against that distinction, a library sentence like "I am an amazing person" is aimed at exactly the wrong target: it argues with the global verdict on the global verdict's own terms, and loses. A sentence you write yourself can be built differently — aimed at the act, sized to what is actually true: "I interrupted her, and interrupting is something I can do less", "the apology is made; a third one would be for me, not for them". Apps that let you write, record and shrink a sentence rank above fixed libraries of large, self-celebrating ones.

2. **Is the tone warmth, or is it triumph?** The helpful voice for shame is not a louder cheerleader; it is the voice you would use to someone you respect who is hurting — steady, specific, on their side without lying for them. That is the clinical intuition behind compassionate mind training, developed for people with high shame and self-criticism who find self-warmth difficult or even frightening (Gilbert & Procter, 2006). It is also what the laboratory evidence demands. Wood, Perunovic and Lee (2009) found that people with low self-esteem who repeated a large positive self-statement — "I'm a lovable person" — felt worse than those who did not, because the gap between the sentence and the belief summoned the counter-evidence. In shame that gap is at its widest, so the size test is strictest here: sentences that offer warmth at a believable size ("I can be a person who did that and still be worth talking to, including by myself") rank above sentences that announce a transformed, flawless self.

3. **Does it reach you in the replay minute, before the hiding?** Shame is fast and it is social: the spike arrives when a face is remembered, a message is re-read, a name lights up the phone. Its action urges — apologise again, explain again, withdraw, delete, disappear — all happen within minutes, on the same phone the app lives on. The practical test is therefore timing and friction. A sentence already on your lock screen, or one press away, can put the act/self separation between the memory and the urge — can turn "send the third apology now" into "read the line first, then decide what repair, if any, is actually owed". An app that needs a programme, a session or a setup project arrives after the apology has been sent and the plans have been cancelled.

4. **What does it cost, and what does a silent month cost you?** Unlearning a global verdict is measured in months, not in a trial week, and a habit study at University College London found a new behaviour took a median of 66 days to feel automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days (Lally et al., 2010). Judge every app on the long window: what it costs over a year, and whether returning after three weeks of hiding feels like resuming or like one more failure to confess — because for a person in shame, an app that greets absence with a broken streak has simply become another witness for the prosecution.

## The six at a glance

| App | Best for | Standout | Get it |

## 1. Believe: Best for writing the act-sized sentence yourself, in your own voice

Believe takes first place here because question 1 is the whole game on this page, and Believe is the only app on this list built around letting you set the content of the claim yourself. You can **write your own affirmations**, **record them in your own voice**, and say them to your own face in the **Soul mirror**. That is how a sentence survives contact with a replay. Not "I am a wonderful person", which the replay will dismantle in seconds, but the line that separates the two things shame has fused: the act, named plainly and at its real size — "I was sharp with him because I was tired; sharp is repairable" — and the self, returned to ordinary size — "one tired sentence is not a character". Its listing organises words by the moment you are in, and the named categories include **self-love** and **relationships**, alongside confidence before a hard day, calm before sleep, gratitude, mornings, work, study, health, money, mindfulness and personal growth, and its current listing adds a free "Mental Health" category. **Timed sessions** with music and calming sounds give one line room to land, and widgets and scheduled reminders cover the timing of question 3 — a reminder set for the hour the replay usually starts is a sentence you arranged on a steadier day, before the verdict arrived. Write the lines small, write them about acts and next steps, and let the mirror be practice in being looked at — by yourself, kindly — rather than a performance of a self you do not yet believe.

Believe launched in June 2021 and showed **4.9 stars from 379 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026. Its US listing shows Believe Premium+ at **$3.99 a month** and a **lifetime option at $69.99** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

The crowd is elsewhere — 379 ratings against I am's hundreds of thousands. If social proof is your evidence, the evidence is not here. Believe also tracks consistency with practice medals, which cuts directly against question 4: for most people medals are decoration, but if a broken streak would become one more count in the indictment, use the sessions and ignore the medals entirely. And the writing, the recording and the mirror all ask something of you up front, on a steadier day — including, for a person in shame, the hardest editorial decision on this page: the sentences have to be written about the act, not as a defence of the self, and on the worst evenings even opening the editor may be more than you have. That is why Innertune, which asks for one press, is second on this page.

## 2. Innertune: Best for sentences that arrive with one press in the replay minute

Innertune is the app for the moment when question 1 cannot even be attempted because the replay is already loud and the urge — apologise again, explain again, withdraw — is already moving. Its core practice requires, at the moment of use, exactly one press. Its listing opens with "Stop the negative thought spiral", builds **a personalised playlist for your exact situation** from **77,000 affirmations across 550+ playlists**, and is built to run while you sleep, work or relax. For shame and guilt, that passivity has one specific, honest use: press play in the gap — while the remembered face is on the screen and the third apology is still a draft — and let a steadier sentence occupy the channel while the urge rises, crests and, given minutes rather than verdicts, usually falls. What you do in those minutes is the point: the playlist is a pause with a purpose, and the purpose is deciding what repair, if any, is actually owed — once, in proportion, and then done. Premium lists **19 voices including an ASMR option**, your own-voice recording if you want it later, binaural and sleep beats, a night mode and offline downloads. Its listing names its targets as anxiety and racing thoughts, sleep and restless nights, self-doubt and confidence, and breaking negative thought patterns — the neighbourhood of the replay, even if not its name.

Innertune showed **4.8 stars from 12,174 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026. Its US listing shows premium plans including **$29.99 a year** and **$9.99 a month** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

Listening can become the hiding. If pressing play turns into a way of never sending the one apology that is owed — or, at the other extreme, a ritual you must complete before you are allowed back among people — the app has stopped being a pause and become part of the loop, and the honest move is to notice that and use it less, as a bridge to the proportionate act rather than instead of it. A playlist personalised to a situation is also still not a sentence sized to your belief, and the library's general vocabulary leans toward mindset and momentum; check a playlist's tone on a steadier day, and skip any track whose promise is that you are flawless and misunderstood — on this page, owning the act is the exit, and a sentence that acquits you of everything teaches nothing except dependence on the acquittal. And Innertune is a subscription to listening, indefinitely; if what you need is words you eventually own without the app, start with Believe above.

## 3. I am: Best for a different sentence on the lock screen, at scale

I am is the category default, and its listing starts from a neighbouring observation: "How many negative thoughts have been repeating in your mind?" Its answer is placement and scale. On the App Store since 2014, **4.8 stars from 739,813 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026, it lets you choose daily intentions and set **reminders to be delivered throughout the day**, with widgets and lock-screen lines in a library large enough that the sentence rarely repeats. For shame and guilt, the practical value is interruption at the exact surface where the verdict forms: the lock screen is where the message preview appears, where the unanswered thread gets re-read for coldness, where the decision to hide gets made. A different sentence already there — before you open the thread and start prosecuting — is question 3 done with zero effort, in the seconds where "an act, not a self" is still possible. Set one reminder for the hour the replay usually starts, because that is when this page's reader will meet it. Premium is listed at **$59.99 a year** and **$14.99 a month**, with a **lifetime option at $89.99**, on its US store page.

### Where it falls short

The relationship is one-directional. You receive; you rarely make. There is no mirror, no voice recorder and no way to shrink a sentence until it is believable, so the library's size works against questions 1 and 2 as often as for it: much of the category's general language leans toward achievement, dreams, ambitions and abundance — its listing speaks of verbally affirming your dreams and ambitions and becoming what you believe, and of ensuring every day is an amazing day. Read against question 2, that register is triumph, not warmth: on a shame evening, a large sentence about your amazing self can feel less like comfort than like a description of the person you have just failed to be — the exact backfire Wood and colleagues measured. And nothing in the app helps you do the one thing guilt is actually for — name the act, make the proportionate repair, stop. Use I am for interrupting the replay with sheer variety and placement. For words that separate the act from the self, it does not compete with the two apps above it.

## 4. Gratitude: Best for a written record of what actually happened

Gratitude is built from a private gratitude journal with prompts, a vision board, Daily Zen content, and affirmations you can **listen to or read**, write yourself, set to music and record in your own voice. For shame and guilt, the journal is the active ingredient — used in one specific way, and it is not the way the app's name suggests. Do not use it to count blessings. Use it as the record the prosecuting mind never keeps. Shame edits memory in a particular direction: it keeps the worst ten seconds in high resolution and deletes the rest of the evidence — what you actually said, in full; what the other person actually replied; whether the apology was accepted; whether anyone else even noticed. A dated line, kept brief and factual — "snapped at K. at 15:40; apologised at 16:05; he said forget it and meant it; no second apology sent" — is written evidence, in your own hand, that the act had edges and an ending, and that the global verdict was an edit, not a report. That record is also where question 1 becomes a habit: each entry practises the separation, act first and self second, until the separation starts arriving on its own. Its prompts and reminders lower the cost of starting, and the listing stresses that the journal is completely private — which matters more here than on any other page in this series, because a record of shame written for an audience would be performed, not kept. It showed **4.9 stars from 44,996 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026, and its US listing shows an annual pro plan at **$29.99** and a monthly plan at **$4.99**. It has been on the App Store since 2018.

### Where it falls short

The frame is gratitude, and the frame is a risk. On the evening when the feeling is raw, an app organised around counting good things can feel like an instruction to be thankful instead of accountable — and shame is not an ingratitude problem, and guilt is not cured by blessings. Keep the entries factual — the act, the repair, the outcome, in a line or two — and let the app's sunnier framing stay unused. The vision board and manifestation content point the wrong way for the same reason: a board of the flawless future self is question 2's triumph in picture form. Writing also asks more than listening does: on the worst weeks, the weeks the feeling costs most, the journal will stay closed, and that has to be allowed to cost nothing. And like Believe, its strongest use here — the evidence record — is a use you bring to it, not the use it advertises. If the name of the app itself puts you off in this season, that reaction is information; skip to Innertune or Believe.

## 5. ThinkUp: Best for your own voice saying the separated line, on a loop

ThinkUp's core idea is the one your brain is built to trust: your own voice. You select affirmations from an expert-approved list or use them as inspiration to **create your own**, **record them in your own voice**, add an image that inspires you, set them to music, and loop the programme with notifications to listen daily. For shame and guilt, the own-voice recording is the real offer, for the same reason Believe ranks first: a sentence you wrote, at a size you chose, said in the voice that lives in your head anyway, has a chance of being believed that a stranger's acquittal does not. Record the programme for the specific hour that costs you — the commute home after the meeting, the Sunday evening before the week, the night after any family gathering — because the replay is rarely general; it has times of day. And build the programme the way question 1 requires: let its lines name acts and repairs, in order — "I did X; X was mine; the repair is Y; Y is done or scheduled; the rest is replay, not conscience" — so the loop ends with the account settled rather than with a larger claim about who you are. It has been on the App Store since 2014 and showed **4.7 stars from 7,524 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026. Its US listing shows plans including **$7.99 a month**, **$39.99 a year** and a **lifetime option at $99.99** among its in-app purchases.

### Where it falls short

The framing around that recording is achievement language: its listing opens by asking what stops you from achieving goals or becoming who you want to be, and builds toward motivation, prosperity and success, including manifestation. Read against questions 1 and 2, that vocabulary is pointed the wrong way for this feeling — you are not failing to become someone; you did a specific thing, or believe you did, and the work is proportion, not becoming. The loop format carries a warning specific to this page, in stronger form than Innertune's playlists: a programme played until the feeling lifts can quietly become a penance — listen enough times and you are forgiven — and penance is the loop wearing a kinder costume. Keep it short, keep it factual, and let some evenings end with the repair made and no programme at all: that making is the practice working, not failing. The programme model also assumes setup and daily listening discipline; building it is a project, and projects belong on the steadier days. Used narrowly — one recorded programme, your words, act-sized, played in the hour that costs you — it earns its place.

## 6. Anicca: One short card, no streak, nothing to confess or fall behind on

Anicca is our app, and it is listed last because on the evidence available today, last is where it belongs on this page. What it does is narrow: its listing describes it as **made for anxious, overthinking minds**; you **pick a focus — self-love and confidence are among those named** — and a new affirmation appears on your **Lock Screen every day**, with short cards you can swipe through at your own pace, save, copy or share, across 8 background themes, in six languages. There is no streak to break, no programme to build, no journal to keep up, and nothing that counts a hiding week against you — which, against questions 3 and 4, is the one thing it does exactly right for this feeling: it cannot become one more witness, one more debt, or one more place you have to explain an absence, and it can be left alone for as long as you need and resumed without apology. It does not ask you to face a mirror, write a record, or say anything aloud. On this page, that lightness is a feature, not a slogan. It is iPhone only.

The numbers, stated plainly because this page checks everyone else's: Anicca showed **5.0 stars from 1 US rating** and **4.5 stars from 48 ratings in Japan** when we checked on November 20, 2026. Its US listing shows premium at **$14.99 a month** and **$59.99 a year**. One rating is not social proof of anything, and this page will not dress it up as such.

### Where it falls short

Almost everywhere this page measures. There is no shame or guilt category, no way to write your own words or record your own voice, and no way to shrink a sentence until it separates an act from a self — the exact ability question 1 ranks first. Nothing in it keeps the factual record, walks you through a proportionate repair, or helps you tell conscience from replay, which is the whole skill this feeling requires. Its named focuses are self-love and confidence, which are neighbouring needs, not this one, and some of its general positive language is larger than a shame evening can hold — the Wood et al. warning applies to our own sentences too. If the verdict itself is the thing, Believe and Gratitude above are built closer to it, and the research section below matters more than any app on this page. Anicca fits a narrower moment: you want one kind line, already on the lock screen where the re-read thread also lives, that asks nothing, counts nothing and never demands a confession, from an app small enough to be honest about what it is.

## Also worth knowing: Mantra

Mantra, around since February 2017, showed **4.8 stars from 34,494 US ratings** when we checked on November 20, 2026. Its listing opens from the same observation as this page — "Our brains are wired to repeat negative feelings if fed with negative thoughts" — and is built around a daily affirmation you hold with, plus the ability to **read as many affirmations as you like by swiping**, across **30+ categories**, with smart daytime and bedtime reminders. Its current listing also lets you **add your own affirmations and record your voice**, which moves it closer to question 1 than a pure library. Its US listing shows a monthly plan at **$4.99** and annual plans including **$29.99** among its in-app purchases. It is a credible middle option — a large, established library with a light daily ritual — and the swipe-to-keep-reading form suits the restless replay hour when your hands need something to do that is not re-opening the thread. What keeps it off the main list for this page is focus: its framing is general positivity and manifestation rather than the specific discipline this feeling needs, so its own-words tools arrive inside a library whose default sentences still need the steadier-day tone check described under Believe — keep the ones that name an act and a next step, rewrite or skip the ones that announce a flawless self.

## What the research does — and does not — say

Four findings decide how to use this list, and the first one names the feeling itself. Tangney, Stuewig and Mashek (2007), reviewing the moral-emotions literature, set out the distinction this whole page is built on: **guilt focuses on a specific behaviour** — "I did a bad thing" — and tends to come with empathy for the person affected and urges to confess, apologise and make amends; **shame focuses on the global self** — "I am bad" — and tends to come with feeling small, exposed and worthless, and urges to hide or disappear. Across the studies they review, proneness to guilt, once its overlap with shame is removed, is associated with constructive, reparative patterns, while proneness to shame is associated with hiding, blaming others, anger turned outward or inward, and more psychological symptoms. Read it honestly: this is a distinction between tendencies across many studies, not a diagnosis of a single evening, and ordinary guilt and ordinary shame arrive mixed in real life. What it supports is the diagnostic move of question 1: before choosing words, ask which of the two you are in — because the repair for an act does not repair a self, and a sentence aimed at the self, when the problem is an act, argues with the wrong defendant.

Second, the two feelings do not carry the same weight, and the size of the difference has been pooled. Kim, Thibodeau and Jorgensen (2011) meta-analysed **108 studies with 22,411 participants** and **242 effect sizes**, and found shame more strongly associated with depressive symptoms (**r = .43**) than guilt (**r = .28**). Two details matter as much as the headline. Guilt divorced from a specific, proportionate act carried associations as large as shame's: **generalised guilt** — free-floating guilt with no specific context — at **r = .42**, and guilt built on exaggerated responsibility for uncontrollable events at **r = .39**. And **external shame** — seeing yourself negatively through the imagined eyes of others — carried the largest association of all, at **r = .56**. Hold the limit as firmly as the numbers: the authors state plainly that these correlational data are ambiguous about causation; shame does not stand convicted of causing depression by this paper. What the pattern supports is narrower and still useful: guilt earns its keep only while it stays attached to a specific act you can repair — the moment it generalises into "I am guilty of everything, somehow", it weighs what shame weighs. That is the research form of this page's first question.

Third, warmth is trainable, and the founding evidence for training it is small — stated at its real size. Gilbert and Procter (2006) developed compassionate mind training for people with high shame and self-criticism, whose difficulties tend to be chronic and who often find self-warmth and self-acceptance difficult or frightening. In their pilot, **six patients** attending a day centre for chronic difficulties completed **12 two-hour group sessions**, and showed significant reductions in depression, anxiety, self-criticism, shame, inferiority and submissive behaviour, alongside an increased ability to be self-soothing. Hold every limit: six people, no control group, a clinical day-centre population, a therapy delivered by clinicians — not an app, and not evidence that an app does this. What it supports is only the direction of question 2: the voice that helps in shame is a soothing, affiliative one, deliberately practised, and for people whose shame is chronic or fused with other conditions, the practising belongs in therapy of this kind, with a person, not in a subscription.

Fourth, the size of the sentence is not a detail; it is the mechanism of failure. Wood, Perunovic and Lee (2009) showed in two experiments that participants with low self-esteem who repeated the positive self-statement "I'm a lovable person", or focused only on how it was true, **felt worse** than those who did not repeat it or who were allowed to consider how it was both true and not true — while participants with high self-esteem benefited slightly. The authors' own warning names the exact sentences this feeling attracts: outlandish, unreasonably positive self-statements, such as "I accept myself completely", may harm the very people they are designed for. Shame is low self-regard at its most acute and most specific, so this page applies the finding at full strength: any app whose default move is a global claim about the self must be used, if at all, with its own-words tools and its smallest sentences — and a sentence that leaves you feeling worse is not a sentence to push through. It is a sentence to shrink, or to drop.

The boundary, stated plainly. Shame and guilt, by themselves, are not diagnoses, and nothing on this page is a treatment for any condition, including our own app. But either feeling can sit inside larger things. If shame is there most days for months; if you are withdrawing from work, people and care; if it arrives with persistent low mood, trauma memories, disordered eating, or thoughts of harming yourself — that is a conversation for a clinician, or, in a crisis, your local emergency number or crisis line now (in the US, call or text 988; in Japan, 110 or 119 in an emergency). And the boundary runs in the other direction too: if you have actually harmed someone, an app is not the repair. The apology, the restitution and the changed behaviour are — once, in proportion, and addressed to them, not performed for the feeling. Structured human help, and honest human repair, both have more support behind them than any app on this page.

The habit research points the same way as in our other comparisons. Lally et al. (2010) found a new behaviour took a median of 66 days to feel automatic, with a range of 18 to 254 days. A counter-practice — naming the act, sizing the repair, writing the record, letting the account close — is still being built in month two, which is why question 4, what it costs over a year and what a silent month costs you, outranks every feature list. A smaller app that costs nothing to resume beats a complete app you stopped opening because resuming it felt like one more thing to be ashamed of.

## How to choose

- **You want words that are actually yours — act-sized, written by you, at your size, in your voice, said to your own face:** Believe.
- **The replay spikes and you need sentences that arrive with one press, in the gap before the third apology or the disappearance:** Innertune.
- **You want the biggest library and the most social proof, interrupting on your lock screen where the re-read thread lives:** I am.
- **Writing down what actually happened — the act, the repair, the outcome — is how you push back against the global verdict:** Gratitude.
- **Your own voice on a loop is the requirement, and you have a steadier week coming in which to set it up for the hour that costs you:** ThinkUp.
- **You want one short card, on the focus you chose, with no streak to break, nothing to confess, and nothing that counts a hiding week against you:** Anicca.
